title_en: Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. et al. v. Conversant Wireless Licensing Co., Ltd. — dispute over confirmation of non-infringement of patent rights and standard essential patent licensing
ruling_gist_en: 1. For an application for behavior preservation with the nature of an "anti-suit injunction," the people's court shall examine it in accordance with Article 100 of the Civil Procedure Law and Article 7 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Review of Behavior Preservation Cases in Intellectual Property Disputes, focusing on factors such as whether the respondent's initiation of a lawsuit or application for enforcement of a judgment in a foreign court will have a substantial impact on the trial and enforcement of the Chinese lawsuit, and whether the adoption of behavior preservation measures complies with the principle of international comity. Regarding whether the respondent's initiation of a lawsuit or application for enforcement of a judgment in a foreign court will have a substantial impact on the trial and enforcement of the Chinese lawsuit, consideration may be given to whether the parties in the Chinese and foreign lawsuits are substantially the same, whether the subject matters of the trials overlap, and whether the effect of the respondent's extraterritorial litigation conduct will interfere with the Chinese lawsuit. Regarding the principle of international comity, consideration may be given to the chronological order of case acceptance, the appropriateness of jurisdiction, and whether the impact on the foreign court's trial and judgment is moderate.

full_text_en:
Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. et al. v. Conversant Wireless Licensing S.à r.l.

— Dispute over confirmation of non-infringement of patent rights and standard essential patent licensing

Ruling Summary

I. For an application for behavioral preservation that is essentially in the nature of an anti-suit injunction, the people's court shall review it in accordance with Article 100 of the Civil Procedure Law and Article 7 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Review of Behavioral Preservation Cases in Intellectual Property Disputes, with a focus on factors such as whether the respondent's initiation of a lawsuit or application for enforcement of a foreign court judgment in a foreign court will have a substantial impact on the trial and enforcement of the Chinese action, and whether the adoption of behavioral preservation measures complies with the principle of international comity. In considering whether the respondent's initiation of a lawsuit or application for enforcement of a foreign court judgment in a foreign court will have a substantial impact on the trial and enforcement of the Chinese action, factors to be considered include whether the parties in the Chinese and foreign actions are substantially the same, whether the subject matters of the trials overlap, and whether the effects of the respondent's foreign litigation conduct would interfere with the Chinese action. In considering the principle of international comity, factors to be considered include the order in which the cases were filed, the appropriateness of jurisdiction, and the propriety of the impact on the trial and judgment of the foreign court.

II. A behavioral preservation measure that prohibits the respondent from performing a certain act has a special nature. If the respondent refuses to comply with the obligation of inaction set forth in the behavioral preservation ruling and illegally commits an act that changes the original state, such intentional illegal conduct constitutes a continuous violation of the behavioral preservation ruling and a continuous change of the original state. Such conduct shall be deemed as an illegal act committed each day, and a daily fine may be imposed and accumulated on a daily basis as appropriate.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2019) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong Zi Nos. 732, 733, and 734-1

Applicant (Appellee, Plaintiff at First Instance): Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. Domicile: Huawei Headquarters Office Building, Bantian, Longgang District, Shenzhen City, Guangdong Province, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Zhao Minglu, Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Zhao Ye, Attorney at Beijing Jingtian & Gongcheng Law Firm.

Agent ad litem (Case No. 732): Wang Bin, male, employee of the Company.

Agent ad litem (Case No. 733): Wu Xiaoqian, female, employee of the Company.

Agent ad litem (Case No. 734): Tan Weifeng, male, employee of the Company.

Respondent (Appellant, Defendant at First Instance): Conversant Wireless Licensing S.à r.l. Domicile: 12 Rue Jean Engling, L-1474 Luxembourg, Grand Duchy of Luxembourg.

Authorized Representative: Nicholas Procopenko, Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Peng Fei, Attorney at Beijing Zhongzi Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wang Xiaojing, Attorney at Beijing Zhongzi Law Firm.

In the three cases concerning disputes over confirmation of non-infringement of patent rights and standard essential patent licensing between the appellant Conversant Wireless Licensing S.à r.l. (hereinafter referred to as Conversant) and the appellees Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huawei Technologies), Huawei Terminal Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huawei Terminal), and Huawei Software Technologies Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huawei Software), the applicant Huawei Technologies filed an application for behavioral preservation with this Court on August 27, 2020, requesting an order that the respondent Conversant shall not apply for enforcement of the injunction judgment rendered by the Düsseldorf Regional Court (hereinafter referred to as the Düsseldorf Court) in the case of Conversant v. Huawei Technologies, Huawei Technologies Germany GmbH, and Huawei Technologies Düsseldorf GmbH (hereinafter collectively referred to as Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates) concerning infringement of standard essential patents, pending the final judgment of this Court in these three cases. Shenzhen Huawei Branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Limited provided a guarantee for the above behavioral preservation application of Huawei Technologies, issuing a guarantee letter No. 0400000560-2020 (Guarantee) Zi No. 0841, with a guarantee amount of RMB 19.7 million.

Huawei Technologies stated that on April 20, 2018, Conversant filed a lawsuit with the Düsseldorf Court (hereinafter referred to as the German Action), alleging that Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates infringed Conversant's standard essential patents with European Patent Nos. EP1797659, EP1173986, and EP1878177, requesting the Düsseldorf Court to prohibit Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates from selling, using, importing, or possessing related mobile terminal products, to disclose relevant infringement and sales information, to compensate for infringement damages, to destroy and recall infringing products, and to bear litigation costs. The European patents asserted by Conversant in the German Action are respectively family patents of the Chinese patents with Patent Nos. ZL200580038621.8, ZL00804203.9, and ZL200680014086.7 asserted in these three cases. On August 27, 2020, the Düsseldorf Court rendered a judgment prohibiting Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates from selling, using, importing, or possessing related mobile terminal products in Germany. Huawei Technologies claimed that, under German law, Conversant could apply for provisional enforcement of the first-instance judgment upon providing security. Once Conversant submits an enforcement application to the Düsseldorf Court, Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates would either be forced to exit the German market or be forced to accept Conversant's offer of a standard essential patent licensing fee that is more than ten times the rate determined in the first-instance judgments of these three cases, causing irreparable harm to Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates and making it difficult to enforce the final judgments of these three cases concerning Chinese standard essential patent licensing rates. Therefore, it is necessary to prohibit Conversant from applying for enforcement of the Düsseldorf Court's injunction judgment pending the final judgment of these three cases.

This Court finds upon examination:

(I. Status of the Chinese Actions)

On January 25, 2018, Huawei Technologies, Huawei Terminal, and Huawei Software (hereinafter collectively referred to as Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates) filed these three cases with the Nanjing Intermediate People's Court of Jiangsu Province (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance), which accepted and docketed the cases on the same day, with case numbers (2018) Su 01 Min Chu No. 232, (2018) Su 01 Min Chu No. 233, and (2018) Su 01 Min Chu No. 234. Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates requested a judgment: 1. Confirming that their acts of manufacturing, selling, and offering for sale mobile terminal products in China do not infringe the invention patent rights owned by Conversant under Patent Nos. ZL00819208.1, ZL200580038621.8, and ZL200680014086.7. 2. Requesting that for all Chinese essential patents owned or entitled to license by Conversant that are claimed and actually meet 2G, 3G, or 4G standards or technical specifications and are actually implemented by Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates, a judgment be made confirming the licensing conditions, including royalty rates, that comply with the fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) principle for products of Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates.

On September 16, 2019, the court of first instance rendered judgments (2018) Su 01 Min Chu No. 232, 233, and 234: 1. The claim of Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates for confirmation that their acts of manufacturing, selling, and offering for sale mobile terminal products in China do not infringe Conversant's invention patent rights under Patent Nos. ZL00819208.1, ZL200580038621.8, and ZL200680014086.7 was not supported; 2. The licensing of standard essential patents between Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates and Conversant shall be determined on the following conditions: (1) Licensed Patents: All Chinese essential patents owned or entitled to license by Conversant that are claimed and actually meet 2G, 3G, or 4G standards or technical specifications and are actually implemented by Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates. (2) Licensed Products: Mobile terminal products of Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates, namely mobile phones and tablet computers with cellular communication functions. (3) Licensed Acts: Manufacturing, selling, offering for sale, importing licensed products, and using licensed patents on licensed products. (4) Licensing Royalty Rate: For the above licensed acts, the royalty rate payable by Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates to Conversant is: for single-mode 2G or 3G mobile terminal products, the licensing rate for the Chinese patent package, i.e., Chinese standard essential patents, is 0; for single-mode 4G mobile terminal products, the licensing rate for the Chinese patent package, i.e., Chinese standard essential patents, is 0.00225%; for multi-mode 2G/3G/4G mobile terminal products, the licensing rate for the Chinese patent package, i.e., Chinese standard essential patents, is 0.0018%. Furthermore, Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates only need to pay the above licensing rate to Conversant for 4G mobile terminal products containing the technical solution of Patent No. ZL200380102135.9.

Conversant appealed against the judgments of the court of first instance to this Court. This Court accepted and docketed the cases on November 18, 2019, with case numbers (2019) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong Zi No. 732, (2019) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong Zi No. 733, and (2019) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong Zi No. 734, and the three cases are currently being tried.

(II. Status of the German Action)

On April 20, 2018, Conversant filed a lawsuit with the Düsseldorf Court against Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates concerning infringement of standard essential patent rights. The patents in question are European Patent Nos. EP1797659, EP1173986, and EP1878177, which are respectively family patents of the Chinese patents involved in these cases, namely ZL200580038621.8, ZL00804203.9, and ZL200680014086.7. Conversant requested the Düsseldorf Court to prohibit Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates from selling, using, importing, or possessing related mobile terminal products, to disclose relevant infringement and sales information, to compensate for infringement damages, to destroy and recall infringing products, and to bear litigation costs.

On August 27, 2020, the Düsseldorf Court rendered a first-instance judgment, finding that Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates infringed Conversant's European Patent No. EP1797659, and ordered them to cease providing, selling, using, or importing or possessing related mobile terminals for such purposes, to cease offering or delivering mobile phones and tablet computers with UMTS standard functions to customers, to provide information on relevant infringement and sales activities, to destroy and recall infringing products, and to bear litigation costs. The judgment could be provisionally enforced upon provision of security of EUR 2.4 million. The judgment found that Conversant's offer of a standard essential patent licensing fee to Huawei Technologies did not violate the FRAND principle. The rate for multi-mode 2G/3G/4G mobile terminal products in the aforementioned offer of Conversant was approximately 18.3 times the Chinese standard essential patent licensing rate determined in the first-instance judgments of these three cases.

(III. Status of Rights Validity of Related Chinese Family Patents)

European Patent No. EP1797659 is a family patent of Chinese Patent No. ZL200580038621.8. On August 8, 2018, the National Intellectual Property Administration issued Invalidation Request Examination Decision No. 36922, declaring all claims of Chinese Patent No. ZL200580038621.8 invalid. Conversant disagreed and filed an administrative lawsuit with the Beijing Intellectual Property Court, and the patent validation administrative case is currently under trial.

This Court, upon examination, considers that Huawei Technologies' application to prohibit Conversant from applying for enforcement of the Düsseldorf Court's judgment pending the final judgment of this Court in these three cases is essentially an application for behavioral preservation. For an application for behavioral preservation that prohibits the enforcement of a foreign court judgment, a comprehensive judgment should be made considering the following factors: the impact of the respondent's application for enforcement of the foreign court judgment on the Chinese action, whether the adoption of behavioral preservation measures is indeed necessary, whether the harm to the applicant from not adopting behavioral preservation measures exceeds the harm to the respondent from adopting such measures, whether the adoption of behavioral preservation measures would harm the public interest, and whether the adoption of behavioral preservation measures conforms to the principle of international comity.

(A. Impact of the Respondent's Application for Enforcement of the Foreign Court Judgment on the Chinese Action)

For an applicant seeking behavioral preservation to prohibit the respondent from applying for enforcement of a foreign court judgment, the people's court should first examine whether the respondent's implementation of such conduct would have a substantial impact on the trial and enforcement of the judgment in the Chinese action. If the respondent's relevant conduct may impede the trial of the Chinese action or make the enforcement of the Chinese judgment difficult, prohibitive preservation measures may be taken against such conduct. Specifically for these three cases: First, from the perspective of litigation parties, the parties in these three cases are Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates and Conversant, while the parties in the German Action are Conversant and Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates. The parties in both actions are substantially the same. Second, from the perspective of the subject matter of the trial, in these three cases, Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates seek to determine the royalty rate for Conversant's Chinese standard essential patents. In the German Action, Conversant alleges that Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates infringe Conversant's standard essential patents and requests the Düsseldorf Court to order them to cease infringement. The injunction judgment rendered by the Düsseldorf Court is premised on the finding that Conversant's licensing fee offer made during negotiations with Huawei Technologies and others complied with the FRAND principle. Therefore, although there are differences in the nature of the disputes between these three cases and the German Action, the subject matters of the trials partially overlap. Finally, from the perspective of the effect of the conduct, if Conversant applies for enforcement of the Düsseldorf Court's injunction judgment and it is granted, it would interfere with the trial of these three cases and would likely render the trial and judgment of these three cases meaningless. In summary, Conversant's act of applying for enforcement of the Düsseldorf Court's injunction judgment will have a substantial negative impact on the progression of the trial and enforcement of the judgment in these three cases. Huawei Technologies' application to this Court to prohibit Conversant from implementing the above conduct meets the prerequisite for such behavioral preservation.

(B. Whether the Adoption of Behavioral Preservation Measures Is Indeed Necessary)

In examining whether the adoption of behavioral preservation measures is necessary, the focus should be on whether not adopting such measures would cause irreparable harm to the legal rights and interests of the applicant or make it difficult to enforce the judgment in the case. In principle, prohibitive preservation measures should only be taken when truly necessary. In these three cases, the Düsseldorf Court's injunction judgment has been rendered. Once Conversant applies for and obtains enforcement, under this urgent situation, Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates would have only two options: either be forced to exit the German market or be forced to accept Conversant's terms and reach a settlement. In the former scenario, the market losses and lost business opportunities suffered by Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates due to exiting the German market cannot be compensated by monetary means after the fact. In the latter scenario, under the pressure of the injunction judgment, Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates would have to accept Conversant's offer of a rate 18.3 times that determined by the court of first instance and would likely be forced to abandon the opportunity for legal relief in these three cases. Regardless of the determination of the Chinese rate in these three cases, the judgments in the three cases would in fact be difficult to enforce. In either scenario, the harm suffered by Huawei Technologies would be irreparable. These three cases have the necessity for adopting behavioral preservation measures, and the circumstances are indeed urgent.

(C. Reasonable Balancing of the Respective Interests of the Applicant and the Respondent)

In determining whether to adopt behavioral preservation measures prohibiting the respondent from performing a specific act, a balance must also be struck between the harm to the applicant from not adopting the measures and the harm to the respondent from adopting the measures, taking into account the interests of both parties. If the harm to the applicant from not adopting the measures exceeds the harm to the respondent from adopting the measures, the adoption of behavioral preservation measures may be deemed reasonable. Moreover, the greater the extent to which the harm to the applicant from not adopting the measures exceeds the harm to the respondent from adopting the measures, the stronger the reasonableness of adopting the preservation measures. In these three cases, as stated above, once Conversant applies for and obtains enforcement of the Düsseldorf Court's injunction judgment, if this Court does not adopt corresponding behavioral preservation measures, Huawei Technologies would suffer irreparable harm, including being forced to exit the German market or forced to accept the licensing offer and abandon legal relief in Chinese courts. In contrast, if this Court adopts behavioral preservation measures, the harm to Conversant would merely be the temporary suspension of enforcement of the Düsseldorf Court's first-instance judgment. The Düsseldorf Court's judgment is not final, and temporarily suspending its enforcement does not affect Conversant's other litigation rights in Germany. At the same time, Conversant is the owner of standard essential patents, and its core interest in the German Action is to obtain monetary compensation. The harm caused to Conversant by temporarily suspending enforcement of the Düsseldorf Court's injunction judgment is relatively limited. Comparing the two, the harm to Huawei Technologies from not adopting behavioral preservation measures clearly exceeds the harm to Conversant from adopting such measures. Therefore, adopting behavioral preservation measures is reasonable. Additionally, Shenzhen Huawei Branch of Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Limited has provided corresponding security for Huawei Technologies' behavioral preservation application, which can lawfully protect Conversant's interests.

(D. Whether the Adoption of Behavioral Preservation Measures Would Harm the Public Interest)

In determining whether to adopt behavioral preservation measures prohibiting the respondent from performing a specific act, it is also necessary to examine whether the adoption of such measures would harm the public interest. These three cases and the related German Action primarily involve the interests of Huawei Technologies and Conversant. Moreover, in these three cases, the object of the behavioral preservation is to prohibit Conversant from applying for enforcement of the Düsseldorf Court's injunction judgment pending the final judgment of this Court, which does not affect the public interest. In summary, adopting behavioral preservation measures in these three cases will not harm the public interest.

(E. Consideration of International Comity Factors)

For a behavioral preservation application that seeks to prohibit a party from applying for enforcement of a foreign court judgment or from seeking judicial remedies abroad, when reviewing whether to grant such application, considerations of international comity should also be taken into account. In considering international comity, factors such as the chronological order of case acceptance, the appropriateness of jurisdiction, and the degree of impact on the proceedings and judgment of the foreign court may be examined. In terms of the timing of acceptance, the court of first instance accepted the three cases at issue in January 2018, while the Düsseldorf Court accepted the related German proceedings in April 2018, with the three cases having been accepted first. Furthermore, prohibiting Conversant from applying to the Düsseldorf Court for enforcement of the relevant judgment before the final judgment of the three cases is rendered will neither affect the subsequent progress of the German proceedings nor diminish the legal effect of the German judgment; it merely postpones the enforcement of the judgment, and the impact on the proceedings and judgment of the Düsseldorf Court remains within an appropriate scope.

Because the three cases are urgent, this Court must issue a ruling within forty-eight hours; accordingly, Conversant's opinions were not heard in advance. After receiving this ruling, Conversant has the right to apply for reconsideration.

In summary, Huawei Technologies' application for behavioral preservation has factual and legal basis, and this Court grants it. Pursuant to Articles 100, 102, Paragraph 1, Item 6 of Article 111, and Paragraph 1 of Article 115 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling is as follows:

Conversant Wireless Licensing S. à r.l. shall not, before this Court renders a final judgment in the three cases, apply for enforcement of the first-instance injunction judgment rendered by the Regional Court of Düsseldorf, Federal Republic of Germany, on August 27, 2020.

In the event of violation of this ruling, from the date of violation, a daily fine of RMB 1,000,000 shall be imposed, accumulating daily.

The case application fee of RMB 5,000 shall be borne by Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd.

This ruling shall take immediate effect.

If any party disagrees with this ruling, it may apply to this Court for one reconsideration within five days from the date of receipt of the ruling. The enforcement of the ruling shall not be suspended during the reconsideration period.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2019) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong Zi Nos. 732, 733, and 734 (II)

Applicant for Reconsideration: Conversant Wireless Licensing S. à r.l. Address: 12 Jean Engling Street, Luxembourg City, Grand Duchy of Luxembourg.

Authorized Representative: Nicholas Procopenko, Manager of the Company.

Agent Ad Litem: Peng Fei, Attorney at Law, Beijing Zhongzi Law Firm.

Agent Ad Litem: Wang Xiaojing, Attorney at Law, Beijing Zhongzi Law Firm.

Respondent: Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. Address: Huawei Headquarters Office Building, Bantian, Longgang District, Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Zhao Minglu, Manager of the Company.

Agent Ad Litem: Zhao Ye, Attorney at Law, Beijing Jingtian & Gongcheng Law Firm.

Agent Ad Litem (Case No. 732): Wang Bin, male, employee of the Company.

Agent Ad Litem (Case No. 733): Wu Xiaoqian, female, employee of the Company.

In the three cases of dispute over confirmation of non-infringement of patent rights and standard essential patent licensing between the appellant Conversant Wireless Licensing S. à r.l. (hereinafter referred to as Conversant) and the respondents Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huawei Technologies), Huawei Terminal Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huawei Terminal), and Huawei Software Technologies Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huawei Software), this Court issued a civil ruling on behavioral preservation (2019) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong Zi Nos. 732, 733, and 734 (I) (hereinafter referred to as the original ruling) on August 28, 2020. Conversant, disagreeing with the ruling, filed an application for reconsideration with this Court on September 2, 2020. On September 4, 2020, this Court held a hearing on the reconsideration application. Conversant's agents ad litem Peng Fei and Wang Xiaojing, Huawei Technologies' agents ad litem Zhao Ye, Wang Bin, and Wu Xiaoqian, and Huawei Terminal's agent ad litem Chen Guo attended the hearing. The reconsideration of the three cases has now been concluded.

Conversant's application for reconsideration states:

(1) The original ruling restricts Conversant's right under German law to apply for enforcement of the injunction judgment (hereinafter referred to as the German judgment) rendered by the Regional Court of Düsseldorf, Germany (hereinafter referred to as the German Court) in the case of Conversant v. Huawei Technologies, Huawei Technologies Germany GmbH, and Huawei Technologies Düsseldorf GmbH (hereinafter collectively referred to as Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates) concerning infringement of standard essential patents (hereinafter referred to as the German proceedings). This not only violates the principle of Chinese law that the effect of judicial rulings should be limited to the territory of China, but also constitutes a violation of German law. If the original ruling is not revoked, it will endanger the international judicial order, resulting in the possibility that any infringement judgment rendered by a court of any country under its national patent law may not be enforceable within that country.

(2) The original ruling should not restrict Conversant's lawful right to apply to the German Court for enforcement of the judgment. Chinese courts have no jurisdiction over German patent infringement cases, nor do they have jurisdiction over issues related to the application for enforcement of judgments in Germany. The German Court has already determined that Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates have committed infringement and ordered them to cease the infringement. Conversant's request to apply for enforcement of the German judgment is based on the German proceedings and the German portion of the European patent. The German Court has exclusive jurisdiction, and Chinese courts have no jurisdiction. Enforcement of the German judgment is also an important part of the German proceedings, over which Chinese courts have no jurisdiction. Therefore, the behavioral preservation should not restrict Conversant's lawful rights and interests.

(3) Conversant's application to the German Court for enforcement of the German judgment will not render the judgments in the three cases difficult to enforce. First, the three cases are actions for confirmation. Even if the court determines the licensing rate in the three cases, the judgment will not give rise to an obligation to pay, so there is no enforceable content. Second, the subject matter of the three cases and the German proceedings do not overlap. The German judgment is not a judgment on standard essential patent licensing; it does not make a clear determination of the fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) licensing conditions between the parties, but is merely a routine patent infringement judgment. Therefore, there is no conflict between the cases accepted by the German court and the three cases. The enforcement of the German judgment will not have a substantial impact on the proceedings and subsequent judgment of the three cases. Third, the original ruling conflicts with the view expressed in this Court's ruling on jurisdiction objection (2019) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong Guan Yi Zi No. 157 (hereinafter referred to as the No. 157 jurisdiction objection ruling) issued on August 21, 2020.

(4) Conversant's application to the German Court for enforcement of the German judgment will not cause irreparable harm to Huawei Technologies' lawful rights and interests. First, the legal consequences borne by Huawei Technologies under the German judgment constitute a legal obligation, not a loss suffered by it. Second, there is no evidence to prove the existence of the alleged "irreparable harm." Third, Conversant's provision of a guarantee of EUR 2.4 million before applying for enforcement of the German judgment can compensate for any loss Huawei Technologies may suffer. Finally, even if Conversant does not apply for enforcement of the German judgment due to the original ruling, and even if a final judgment in the three cases is subsequently rendered, the German Court will not consider the licensing rate determined by the Chinese judgment, and the German proceedings will not be affected by the Chinese proceedings. Therefore, the issuance of the original ruling cannot avoid the alleged "irreparable harm" claimed by Huawei Technologies.

(5) The original ruling did not reasonably balance the interests of Conversant and Huawei Technologies. First, the original ruling failed to give sufficient consideration to Conversant's interests. Second, Huawei Technologies could avoid the alleged consequences such as withdrawal from the German market by paying licensing fees; such interests are essentially economic interests. Third, the original ruling confused the legal interests that Huawei Technologies should be protected in the three cases with its maximum commercial interests, exceeding the scope of protectable interests defined by Chinese law.

(6) The original ruling's imposition of a fine on a "daily penalty" basis violates Article 115 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Civil Procedure Law).

(7) The original ruling violates Article 104 of the Civil Procedure Law. Conversant is required to provide a security deposit for provisional enforcement in the German Court. According to Article 104 of the Civil Procedure Law, the preservation measures in the three cases should be lifted.

In summary, Conversant requests the revocation of the original ruling.

Huawei Technologies' defense states:

(1) The original ruling complies with international judicial principles and practices and does not affect the jurisdiction of the German Court over the German proceedings. First, the original ruling neither evaluates the legality of the German Court's judgment nor interferes with the substantive trial of the German Court; its target is Conversant's conduct. Second, the ruling conforms to internationally accepted judicial practices and satisfies the constituent elements of relevant cases, with no possibility of affecting the international judicial order. Third, the original ruling has fully considered factors of international comity, and its impact on foreign courts is within an appropriate scope. Fourth, judging from Conversant's past litigation history, it does not believe that an anti-suit injunction would affect the judicial jurisdiction of other countries or endanger the international judicial order. Conversant has applied for similar injunctions in other cases, apparently without considering the harm or disruption such injunctions might cause to China's judicial jurisdiction and the international judicial order.

(2) The original ruling correctly and appropriately restricts Conversant's right to apply for enforcement of the German injunction. In the three cases, if Conversant applies to the German Court for enforcement of the relevant judgment, it would render the judgments in the three cases difficult to enforce, thereby seriously harming Huawei Technologies' right to obtain a ruling from a Chinese court. The temporary restriction on Conversant's exercise of the relevant right is clearly proper and necessary.

(3) The original ruling's finding that applying for enforcement of the German judgment would make the three cases difficult to enforce is correct. First, Conversant's view that the judgments in the three cases lack enforceable content is erroneous. The three cases involve determining the licensing conditions and rates for Chinese standard essential patents and are clearly enforceable. Second, the subject matter of the three cases and the German proceedings overlap to some extent. Although the German judgment is an infringement judgment, it evaluates the negotiation conduct of the parties and whether Conversant's offer complies with FRAND principles. If the German judgment is enforced, Huawei Technologies would be forced to accept Conversant's demanded price, making the judgments in the three cases difficult to enforce. Third, the No. 157 jurisdiction objection ruling only clarifies that domestic courts do not lose jurisdiction due to overlapping proceedings in foreign courts; it clearly cannot support the conclusion that overlapping foreign proceedings will not have an improper impact domestically. Conversant has obviously misconstrued that ruling.

(4) The original ruling fully considered the balance of interests between Huawei Technologies and Conversant. First, if the behavioral preservation measure is not taken, Huawei Technologies' lawful right to sue would suffer irreparable harm. Huawei Technologies' mobile phones and tablets are almost entirely produced in China. According to IDC statistics, in 2019, Chinese sales accounted for 64.23% of Huawei's global sales, while German sales accounted for only 2.39%. Huawei Technologies has the right to request a Chinese court to determine the FRAND licensing rate for Chinese standard essential patents. The deprivation of such right to sue is extremely serious harm to Huawei Technologies. Second, if the behavioral preservation measure is not taken, Huawei Technologies' lawful rights would be disproportionately harmed. Patent licensing fees account for only a small portion of product costs. If the German judgment is enforced, Huawei Technologies would be forced to withdraw from the German market, suffering losses tens or even hundreds of times the licensing fees for the European patents involved in the German proceedings—a loss that no rational commercial entity would find acceptable. Third, the original ruling will not cause harm to Conversant. The original ruling does not permanently prevent Conversant from enforcing the injunction; it only postpones enforcement. The Chinese court will determine the consideration that Conversant should receive for its Chinese standard essential patents in the substantive proceedings, and its lawful rights and interests can be protected in accordance with the law.

(5) The original ruling complies with the Civil Procedure Law and relevant judicial interpretations. First, the three cases involve the determination and adjudication of patent infringement and the compliance with FRAND obligations; they are not property disputes. Moreover, whether Conversant has provided a security in the German Court is irrelevant to the three cases, and the behavioral preservation measures determined in the original ruling should not be lifted. Second, the behavioral preservation in the three cases imposes a prohibition on the party from engaging in specific conduct, creating an obligation to forbear. If the party violates this prohibition for multiple consecutive days, it constitutes multiple violations of the prohibition.

In summary, Huawei Technologies contends that Conversant's grounds for reconsideration are untenable and requests that its application for reconsideration be dismissed.

Upon review, this Court finds that, based on Conversant's reconsideration request and Huawei Technologies' defense, the reconsideration proceedings of the three cases involve the following six issues: (1) whether the impact of the original ruling on the German Court's judgment exceeds an appropriate scope; (2) the effect of Conversant's potential application for provisional enforcement of the German Court's first-instance judgment on the proceedings of the three cases; (3) whether Huawei Technologies would face irreparable harm if the original ruling were not issued; (4) whether the original ruling creates an imbalance in the weighing of the parties' interests; (5) whether the three cases satisfy the conditions for lifting preservation measures under Article 104 of the Civil Procedure Law; and (6) whether the original ruling's imposition of a daily fine for violation violates the law. This Court's analysis is as follows:

(1) Whether the impact of the original ruling on the German Court's judgment exceeds an appropriate scope

Conversant argues in its reconsideration that the original ruling restricts Conversant's rights under German law, violates the Chinese legal principle that judicial rulings should have effect only within the territory, and also violates German law. It contends that Chinese courts have no jurisdiction over the German proceedings and their enforcement, and that the original ruling endangers the international judicial order by rendering the judgment of a foreign court unenforceable. In this regard, this Court holds:

First, the original ruling is made in accordance with Chinese law, and the three cases are not subject to German law, let alone capable of violating German law. In the proceedings of the three cases, Huawei Technologies filed an application for behavioral preservation with this Court, which should be reviewed under Article 100 of the Civil Procedure Law of China. German law has no binding effect on the three cases. It is inherent in judicial sovereignty for a court of one country to exercise its adjudicative power based on its own law. Conversant's claim that the original ruling constitutes a violation of German law clearly lacks factual and legal basis.

Second, the original ruling does not involve the exercise of jurisdiction over the German proceedings. Chinese courts have judicial jurisdiction over civil disputes occurring within the territory of China. The original ruling was issued in the course of the three cases based on a party's application and relevant provisions of Chinese law; it is the result of this Court's exercise of Chinese judicial jurisdiction. The original ruling restricts Conversant from applying for provisional enforcement of the German Court's first-instance judgment before this Court renders a final judgment in the three cases. It neither addresses the infringement finding regarding the European patents involved in the German proceedings nor makes any assessment of the German judgment or its enforcement, and certainly does not interfere with the substantive trial or the effect of the German Court's judgment. Conversant's characterization of the original ruling as an exercise of jurisdiction by a Chinese court over the German proceedings and the enforcement of the judgment is a misreading of both jurisdiction and the content of the original ruling. Therefore, Conversant's argument cannot stand.

Third, the original ruling adheres to the principle of international comity and is consistent with international judicial practice. The original ruling fully considered factors of international comity when it was issued and is consistent with international judicial practice. In particular, it considered the potential impact on the German proceedings. The three cases were accepted before the German Court's acceptance of the related case. The original ruling merely postpones Conversant's application for enforcement of the German Court's first-instance judgment; it neither affects the subsequent progress of the German proceedings nor diminishes the legal effect of the German judgment. Conversant's corresponding argument essentially equates the postponement of the application for enforcement of the German Court's first-instance judgment with the negation of the German judgment's effect, and confuses the restriction on Conversant's individual rights with a restriction on the German judgment and its effect. This is erroneous.

Fourth, Conversant's argument is somewhat inconsistent with its prior conduct. This Court notes that in its global litigation activities, Conversant has previously proactively applied to foreign courts for anti-suit injunctions to prohibit specific parties from filing related lawsuits in Chinese courts. Conversant's prior conduct does not appear to suggest that such anti-suit injunctions would have an adverse effect on the judicial jurisdiction of Chinese courts or the international litigation order. Conversant's argument that the original ruling's impact on the German Court's judgment exceeds an appropriate scope, and the specific reasons it provides, are difficult to reconcile with its prior conduct.

Therefore, the impact of the original ruling on the German proceedings and judgment does not exceed an appropriate scope. Conversant's above reconsideration arguments are untenable and are not supported by this Court.

(2) The effect of Conversant's potential application for provisional enforcement of the German Court's first-instance judgment on the proceedings of the three cases

Conversant argues that applying for provisional enforcement of the German judgment will not affect the final judgment in the three cases, that the three cases are declaratory actions and the final judgment will not contain enforceable content, thus failing to satisfy the conditions for applying the behavioral preservation measure of preventing the judgment from becoming difficult to enforce; that the subject matter of the three cases and the German proceedings do not overlap; and that the original ruling conflicts with the No. 157 jurisdiction objection ruling, according to which, even if the German proceedings partially overlap with the three cases in terms of the subject matter of trial, it will not have a substantial adverse effect on the three cases. In this regard, this Court holds:

First, the final judgments in these three cases are enforceable. First, when reviewing an application for act preservation, regarding whether a party's conduct may cause difficulties in enforcing the judgment or other harm, this element should be understood in light of the characteristics of act preservation. Act preservation is preservative and urgent in nature, with the purpose of ensuring that future judgments can be enforced and that the rights and interests determined in the judgment in favor of the applicant can ultimately be realized. Therefore, in the context of act preservation, when examining whether a party's conduct will cause difficulties in enforcing the judgment, the core focus is whether, if preservation measures are not taken and the party carries out the conduct, it can be ensured that the judgment will have binding force and enforceability on the party, and whether the rights and interests determined in the judgment in favor of the applicant can ultimately be realized. The issue of whether the content of the judgment itself is suitable for direct compulsory enforcement is not a consideration when determining whether a party's conduct may cause difficulties in enforcing the judgment. Conversant's assertion that the final judgments in these three cases are not enforceable mistakenly conflates the enforceability of a judgment with whether the content of the judgment is suitable for compulsory enforcement. Second, the final judgments in these three cases will determine the royalty rate for the standard essential patents in question. This rate is binding on both parties and has enforceable content. The core of a dispute concerning the licensing of standard essential patents is the request for the court to determine specific licensing conditions or content, thereby urging the parties to ultimately reach or perform a licensing agreement. After the judgments in these three cases are rendered, each party has the obligation to comply with the royalty rate standard determined by the judgment. Without the consent of the other party, the standard essential patent holder may not demand a royalty rate higher than that determined by the judgment, and the patent implementer may not pay a royalty rate lower than that determined by the judgment. This is an important manifestation of the binding force and enforceability of the final judgments in these three cases. Finally, if Conversant applies for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court, Huawei Technologies may, under the threat of serious consequences such as being forced to withdraw from the German market, be compelled to reach a settlement with Conversant, accepting a royalty rate far higher than that determined by the first-instance judgment in these three cases, thereby rendering this Court's subsequent trial and the royalty rate determined by its judgment unenforceable and meaningless.

Second, there is partial overlap between the subject matter of these three cases and the German litigation. In these three cases, Huawei Technologies and its Chinese affiliates request the determination of the royalty rate for Conversant's Chinese standard essential patents. In the German litigation, Conversant alleges that Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates have infringed Conversant's standard essential patents and requests that the German court order Huawei Technologies and its German affiliates to cease the infringement. The cease-and-desist judgment issued by the German court is premised on the condition that the licensing fee offer made by Conversant, the standard essential patent holder, during negotiations with Huawei Technologies and others complies with the fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) principle. During the hearing in these three cases, Conversant also acknowledged that the German judgment commented on and found that its licensing fee offer, including that for the Chinese region, did not violate the FRAND principle. Therefore, the original ruling's finding that there is partial overlap between the subject matter of these three cases and the German litigation is not improper.

Third, there is no conflict between the original ruling and the jurisdictional ruling in Case No. 157. First, the nature of the jurisdictional ruling in Case No. 157 differs from that of the original ruling, and the focal points of the disputes they address are markedly distinct. The focal point of the dispute between the parties in the jurisdictional ruling in Case No. 157 was whether the Chinese court had jurisdiction over the case, whereas the original ruling in these three cases is an act preservation ruling prohibiting a specific party from engaging in certain conduct; these two rulings address entirely different legal issues. Second, the conclusion asserted by Conversant cannot be derived from the jurisdictional ruling in Case No. 157. In the jurisdictional ruling in Case No. 157, this Court, using the standard of appropriate connection for jurisdiction, held that parallel litigation pending abroad does not affect the Chinese court's jurisdiction over the case. It only commented on whether the Chinese court had jurisdiction over the case and did not address substantive legal issues, let alone the issue of whether partial overlap in the subject matter of international parallel litigation would cause substantial negative effects on the litigation in the other country.

Therefore, the above-mentioned reconsideration arguments of Conversant are difficult to sustain, and this Court does not support them.

(3) Whether Huawei Technologies would face irreparable harm if the original ruling were not made.

Conversant argues in its reconsideration that the legal consequences imposed on Huawei Technologies by the German court's judgment are legal obligations and do not constitute its losses; there is no evidence to prove the existence of the "irreparable harm" alleged by Huawei Technologies; the provision of a 2.4 million euro security by Conversant upon applying for enforcement of the German judgment is sufficient to compensate for Huawei Technologies' losses; and even if Conversant does not apply for enforcement of the German judgment before the final judgments in these three cases are rendered, because the German court will not consider the patent royalty rate determined by the Chinese judgment and the German litigation is not affected by the Chinese litigation, the issuance of the original ruling cannot avoid the "irreparable harm" alleged by Huawei Technologies. In this regard, this Court holds:

First, enforcement of the German judgment may cause irreparable harm to Huawei Technologies. First, in reviewing the act preservation application in these three cases, the focus should be on the harm that may be caused to Huawei Technologies if Conversant applies for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court during the specific period between the issuance of the first-instance judgment by the German court and this Court's ongoing trial of these three cases. During this period, once the first-instance judgment of the German court is enforced, Huawei Technologies will have only two options: either be forced to withdraw from the German market or be forced to accept Conversant's price demand and reach a settlement with it. In the former scenario, it will suffer related market losses and loss of business opportunities. In the latter scenario, it will be forced to accept Conversant's exorbitantly high patent royalty fee demand and may even abandon the judicial remedy available in these three cases. Therefore, the harm that Huawei Technologies may suffer due to Conversant's application for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court includes both tangible material harm and intangible harm such as loss of business opportunities and market interests; both harm to economic interests and harm to litigation interests; and both harm to interests in Germany and harm to interests in China. Second, as shown above, the scope of harm that Huawei Technologies may suffer due to Conversant's application for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court exceeds the scope of the first-instance judgment of the German court and has no direct connection with the legal liability Huawei Technologies should bear under that judgment. Moreover, the legal liability of Huawei Technologies determined by the first-instance judgment of the German court is merely a possibility; whether this liability is currently borne depends on whether Conversant applies for temporary enforcement.

Second, the original ruling's finding that Huawei Technologies may suffer irreparable harm is supported by evidence. According to the provisions of Article 86, paragraph 2, of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Evidence in Civil Procedures, for facts related to procedural matters such as litigation preservation and recusal, if the people's court, based on the parties' explanations and relevant evidence, considers that there is a relatively high probability that the relevant facts exist, it may find that such facts exist. The act preservation applied for by Huawei Technologies falls within the scope of litigation preservation, and the standard of proof for finding relevant facts applies the preponderance of the evidence standard, not the high probability standard. Huawei Technologies provided the first-instance judgment of the German court and gave a reasonable explanation that temporary enforcement of that judgment may cause it the irreparable harm described above. This explanation is consistent with general commercial logic and existing commercial practices and can preliminarily prove the irreparable harm it alleges.

Third, the provision of a 2.4 million euro security by Conversant is not sufficient to compensate for the harm Huawei Technologies may suffer. First, as previously stated, the harm that Huawei Technologies may suffer due to Conversant's application for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court at this specific moment includes tangible and intangible harm, harm to economic interests and harm to litigation interests, and harm to interests in Germany and harm to interests in China. This harm exceeds the scope of the German judgment and has no direct connection with the legal liability Huawei Technologies should bear under that judgment. Second, even if the German judgment finds that a 2.4 million euro security is sufficient to compensate for the harm Huawei Technologies may suffer in Germany, it cannot compensate for the harm to Huawei Technologies' litigation interests in China. Huawei Technologies seeks judicial remedy in these three cases to determine the royalty rate for Conversant's Chinese standard essential patents, which constitutes its litigation interests in China. If the first-instance judgment of the German court is temporarily enforced, Huawei Technologies may be forced to accept the above-mentioned exorbitantly high price and reach a settlement with Conversant in order to retain the German market, thereby inevitably abandoning its judicial remedy in China. Its litigation interests will suffer substantial losses, and the trial of these three cases will be difficult to advance.

Fourth, whether the German court considers the patent royalty rate determined by the Chinese judgment and is affected by the Chinese litigation is irrelevant to the original ruling. First, the intent of the original ruling is, based on Huawei Technologies' application, to postpone Conversant's application for enforcement of the German judgment, thereby maintaining the trial order and enforcement of the judgment in these three cases, not to affect the German litigation or the German judgment. How the German court views the judgment in these three cases and whether the German litigation is affected by the Chinese litigation are not factors considered in issuing the original ruling. Second, the realization of the legal effect of the original ruling does not depend on whether it is recognized and enforced by the German court, but on whether Conversant complies with the legal obligations determined by the original ruling. Finally, the irreparable harm referred to in the original ruling is the harm caused by Conversant's application for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court before the final judgments in these three cases are rendered, and no other. The original ruling is directed at Conversant. As long as Conversant complies with the legal obligations determined by the original ruling and does not apply for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court before the final judgments in these three cases are rendered, the harm can be avoided.

Therefore, the above-mentioned reconsideration arguments of Conversant lack factual and legal basis, and this Court does not support them.

(4) Whether the original ruling's balance of interests between the parties is imbalanced

Conversant argues in its reconsideration that the original ruling did not fully consider and protect its interests; that protecting Huawei Technologies' interests beyond the scope of its claims in the lawsuit constitutes an error in the application of law; and that the original ruling confuses the legal interests that Huawei Technologies should have protected with its maximum business interests, extending them beyond the scope of protectable interests under Chinese law to unlimitedly expand them into Huawei Technologies' maximum business interests. In this regard, this Court holds:

First, the consideration of the parties' interests in an act preservation ruling uses the comparative method of weighing harms, i.e., comparing the harm to the applicant if the act preservation measure is not taken with the harm to the respondent if the measure is taken, choosing the lesser of the two harms. In these three cases, as previously stated, if the act preservation measure is not taken, Huawei Technologies will suffer irreparable harm, including tangible and intangible harm, harm to economic interests and harm to litigation interests, and harm to interests in Germany and harm to interests in China. During the hearing in these three cases, Conversant acknowledged that its core interest in the German litigation is economic interests, specifically the licensing fees for the standard essential patents involved in the German litigation. Comparing the harmed interests of Huawei Technologies with the core interests of Conversant in the German litigation, the original ruling's finding that the harm to Huawei Technologies from not taking the act preservation measure exceeds the harm to Conversant from taking the measure is not improper. The original ruling, after comprehensively considering the above balance of interests and on the premise that Huawei Technologies provided a security equivalent to the amount of the damages claim for patent infringement in Conversant's German litigation, only temporarily postponed Conversant's application for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court, which has already fully considered Conversant's interests.

Second, the scope of the balance of interests in the original ruling is not directly related to the scope of Huawei Technologies' claims in the lawsuit. An act preservation ruling differs from a substantive judgment on the merits. The applicant for act preservation is not limited to the plaintiff, and the harmed interests to be considered are not limited to the plaintiff's claims. When reviewing an act preservation application, the scope and extent of the balance of interests depend on the scope and degree of the impact of the conduct that is the subject of the act preservation application on the applicant and the respondent. In these three cases, Conversant's application for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court is the subject of the act preservation application. The impact of this conduct on Huawei Technologies' interests can all be taken into consideration. The scope of the balance of interests in the original ruling is not improper.

Third, the original ruling did not consider maximizing Huawei Technologies' business interests. First, the original ruling was made based on Huawei Technologies' application and in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Procedure Law on act preservation. What the original ruling considered was the harm that Huawei Technologies may suffer because Conversant, at this specific moment, applied for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court, not the maximization of Huawei Technologies' business interests. Conversant's claim that the original ruling confuses the legal interests that Huawei Technologies should have protected with its maximum business interests is a misinterpretation of the original ruling. Second, in addition to the harm that Huawei Technologies may suffer because Conversant, at this specific moment, applied for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court, the original ruling was more concerned with the interference and obstruction that Conversant's application for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court at this specific moment might cause to the trial and enforcement of these three cases. Furthermore, the original ruling also considered factors such as Conversant's interests and international comity.

Therefore, the above-mentioned reconsideration arguments of Conversant lack factual and legal basis, and this Court does not support them.

(5) Whether these three cases meet the conditions for lifting the preservation measure under Article 104 of the Civil Procedure Law

Conversant argues in its reconsideration that because it is required to provide a security to apply for enforcement of the German judgment, it meets the conditions set forth in Article 104 of the Civil Procedure Law, which states: "In a property dispute case, if the respondent provides a security, the people's court shall rule to lift the preservation measure." Therefore, the act preservation measure in these three cases should be lifted. In this regard, this Court holds:

First, Conversant's provision of a security to the German court does not fall within the circumstances described in Article 104 of the Civil Procedure Law and does not constitute a sufficient condition for lifting the act preservation measure in the original ruling. On the contrary, once Conversant provides a security to the German court and applies for enforcement of the German judgment, it will constitute a violation of the original ruling and should be subject to corresponding penalties.

Second, Article 12 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Review of Act Preservation Cases in Intellectual Property Disputes stipulates that an act preservation measure taken by a people's court shall generally not be lifted because the respondent provides a security, unless the applicant agrees. Accordingly, even if Conversant provides a corresponding security to this Court, the act preservation measure taken in the original ruling cannot be automatically lifted.

Therefore, Conversant's assertion that the act preservation measure should be lifted lacks basis, and this Court does not support it.

(6) Whether the original ruling's imposition of a daily penalty for violating the ruling violates legal provisions

To ensure the effective enforcement of the act preservation measure in the ruling, the original ruling specified the legal consequences for Conversant's failure to comply: "From the date of violation, a daily fine of RMB 1,000,000 shall be imposed, accumulating on a daily basis." Conversant argues that the method of imposing a daily penalty does not comply with legal provisions. In this regard, this Court holds:

First, the method of imposing a daily penalty complies with legal provisions. Article 115 of the Civil Procedure Law stipulates: "The amount of a fine imposed on an entity shall be not less than RMB 50,000 and not more than RMB 1,000,000." An act preservation measure prohibiting the respondent from engaging in certain conduct has its special characteristics. Its core is directed at the respondent's future conduct, requiring them not to engage in certain conduct and not to illegally change the existing state of affairs. If the respondent refuses to comply with the obligations determined by the court's ruling and changes the existing state of affairs, this constitutes a positive and intentional illegal act. Such intentional illegal conduct by the respondent is a continuous violation of the ruling and a continuous change of the status quo. This conduct is markedly different from a one-time, completed illegal act. It should be considered that the respondent commits a separate illegal act each day. For such a daily continuous act that obstructs civil proceedings, the penalty should be determined by imposing a penalty on a daily basis.

Second, the method of imposing a daily penalty is commensurate with the potential consequences of violating the act preservation measure in these three cases. The intensity of compulsory measures against acts obstructing civil proceedings needs to be commensurate with the potential consequences of such acts. In these three cases, if Conversant intentionally violates the original ruling and applies for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court, it may not only seriously harm Huawei Technologies' market interests in Germany, but also force it to abandon the opportunity to seek judicial remedy in Chinese courts. It would also render the judgments in these three cases difficult to enforce and even meaningless. Conversely, once Conversant applies for temporary enforcement of the first-instance judgment of the German court, it may gain a significant advantage in subsequent licensing fee negotiations between the parties and obtain substantial benefits based on that advantage. Therefore, for Conversant's potential intentional violation of the obligations determined by the original ruling, adopting the method of a daily penalty is both commensurate with the degree of malice and the harmful consequences of the illegal act and is necessary to maintain the legal effect of the original ruling.

Therefore, the original ruling's imposition of a daily penalty for violating the ruling complies with legal provisions and is not improper. The above-mentioned reconsideration arguments of Conversant are difficult to sustain, and this Court does not support them.

This Court specifically points out that Huawei Technologies and Conversant have engaged in litigation worldwide due to disputes over the licensing of standard essential patents, and the existence of related international parallel litigation creates complex situations for courts in different jurisdictions during the trial. This Court respects the litigation rights and interests of both parties as well as their right of disposition based on commercial considerations. However, the act preservation measure determined by the original ruling, as an effective ruling, should be respected and enforced by all parties. Both parties should correctly understand and fully fulfill the act preservation measures determined by the original ruling and shall not deny, circumvent, or obstruct the enforcement of the original ruling in any way. In particular, they shall not apply to the German court for an injunction that contradicts the enforcement of the original ruling. This Court will determine whether a violation of the original ruling has occurred based on the specific actions of the parties and the potential impact on the act preservation measures of the original ruling. If a violation of the original ruling is established, sanctions will be imposed in accordance with the law. The principal responsible persons or directly responsible persons shall be fined or detained. If the conduct constitutes a crime, criminal liability shall be pursued in accordance with the law.

In conclusion, the original ruling has clear findings of fact and correct application of law, and this Court upholds it. The reconsideration request of Conversant Wireless Licensing Co., Ltd. lacks factual and legal basis, and this Court does not support it. In accordance with Article 108 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 171 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling is as follows:

The reconsideration request of Conversant Wireless Licensing Co., Ltd. is dismissed.

This ruling shall take effect immediately.
